title: Node.js
tagline: From first script to production: the complete Node.js roadmap
description: Learn Node.js from scratch to hero: the runtime and event loop, core modules, async patterns and streams, building HTTP servers by hand, databases, authentication and security, tooling, testing, performance, real projects, deployment and interview preparation.

topics.title: What is Node.js?
topics.summary: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine and libuv that lets you run JavaScript outside the browser.
topics.description:
**Node.js** is not a language and not a framework. It is a **runtime**: a program that can execute JavaScript on your computer or server, outside the browser.

### The main parts
| Part | Role |
|---|---|
| **V8** | Google's JavaScript engine (same as Chrome). Compiles JS to machine code and runs it. |
| **libuv** | A C library that gives Node the **event loop**, a thread pool and cross-platform async I/O (files, DNS, sockets, timers). |
| **Node core (C++ and JS)** | Built-in modules such as `fs`, `http`, `path`, `crypto`, `stream`. |
| **npm** | The package manager that ships with Node and hosts millions of packages. |

### Why Node is fast for I/O work
Your JavaScript runs on **one main thread**. When you ask for something slow (read a file, query a database, call an API), Node hands the job to the operating system or to libuv's thread pool and keeps going. When the result is ready, a **callback** is queued and the event loop runs it. This is called **non-blocking I/O** and it lets one process serve thousands of connections.

### What Node is good at
* REST and GraphQL APIs, real-time apps (chat, notifications), streaming
* Command line tools, build tools, scripts and automation
* Microservices and backends-for-frontends

### What Node is not ideal for
Long CPU-heavy work on the main thread (video encoding, huge JSON crunching) blocks every other request. Use `worker_threads` or another service for that.

### Browser JS vs Node JS
Node has no `window` or `document`, but it has `process`, `fs`, `http`, `Buffer` and more. The language (ES2023+) is the same.
keyPoints: Node = V8 engine + libuv event loop + core modules
Single-threaded JavaScript with non-blocking I/O
Great for I/O-bound apps, weak for CPU-bound work on the main thread
Same JavaScript language as the browser, different APIs
pitfalls: Calling Node "a framework" or "a language" in interviews
Saying Node is "single threaded" without mentioning the libuv thread pool

interview.q: What is Node.js?
interview.a: An open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime built on the V8 engine. It uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model (libuv) so a single process can handle many concurrent connections.

interview.q: Is Node.js single-threaded?
interview.a: Your JavaScript code runs on one thread (the event loop), but Node itself uses libuv's thread pool (default 4 threads) for things like file system, DNS lookup, zlib and crypto, and you can add threads with worker_threads.

topics.title: Installing Node and nvm
topics.summary: Install Node from nodejs.org or manage many versions with nvm, fnm or Volta and understand LTS releases.
topics.description:
You can install Node in three common ways.

### 1. Official installer
Download from nodejs.org. Choose the **LTS** (Long Term Support) version for projects. The **Current** line has newest features but is short-lived.

### 2. A version manager (recommended)
Real projects need different Node versions. A version manager lets you switch per project:
* **nvm** (macOS/Linux) and **nvm-windows**
* **fnm** (fast, cross-platform, written in Rust)
* **Volta** (pins the version inside `package.json`)

### Release model
Node ships a new major every six months. Even-numbered majors (20, 22, 24) become **LTS** and receive security fixes for about 30 months. Odd-numbered majors are never LTS. Always use an active LTS line in production.

### Check your setup
`node -v` prints the Node version, `npm -v` prints the npm version, `which node` (or `where node` on Windows) shows which binary runs.

### Pinning a version for a project
Create a `.nvmrc` file containing `22` and run `nvm use`. You can also add `"engines": { "node": ">=20" }` in `package.json` to warn people (and CI) about unsupported versions.

### Tips
* Do not install global packages with `sudo`. A version manager keeps everything in your home folder.
* Keep Node updated: old versions stop receiving security patches.
keyPoints: Use an even-numbered LTS version for production
nvm / fnm / Volta let you switch Node versions per project
.nvmrc and the engines field document the required version
node -v and npm -v verify the installation

Installing with sudo and then fighting permission errors

interview.q: What is LTS in Node.js?
interview.a: Long Term Support. Even-numbered releases get about 30 months of bug and security fixes and are recommended for production, while odd releases are short-lived and meant for trying new features.

interview.q: Why use a version manager?
interview.a: Different projects need different Node versions. A manager installs several versions side by side and switches between them without admin rights or conflicts.

topics.title: REPL and Running Scripts
topics.summary: Use the REPL to experiment and the node command (with flags like --watch and --env-file) to run files.
topics.description:
### The REPL
Type `node` with no arguments to start the **REPL** (Read-Eval-Print Loop). It evaluates each line and prints the result. It is perfect for quick experiments.

Useful REPL features:
* `_` holds the last result
* `.help` lists commands, `.editor` lets you paste multi-line code, `.save file.js` and `.load file.js`
* Tab completion works on objects and built-in modules (which are already available, so `fs` works without `require`)
* `.exit` or Ctrl+D quits

### Running a file
`node app.js` runs a script. The `.js` extension may be left out (`node app`) and `node .` runs the file named in `main` of `package.json`.

### Handy flags
| Flag | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `--watch` | Restart when imported files change |
| `--env-file=.env` | Load environment variables from a file |
| `-e "code"` / `-p "expr"` | Run or print an inline expression |
| `--inspect` | Open the debugger |
| `--check` (`-c`) | Syntax check only |
| `--max-old-space-size=4096` | Raise heap limit (MB) |
| `-r module` / `--import module` | Preload a module |

### Passing arguments
Anything after the file name goes to `process.argv`: `node app.js --port 4000`.

### Running TypeScript
Recent Node versions (22.18+ and 24) can run `.ts` files that use only erasable type syntax with plain `node file.ts` (type stripping, no type checking).

### Exit codes
`0` means success; any other number means failure. Shells and CI use this to detect errors.
keyPoints: node with no args opens the REPL, node file.js runs a script
--watch and --env-file replace nodemon and dotenv for simple cases
Arguments after the file name are available in process.argv
Exit code 0 means success, non-zero means failure

Forgetting that ES module files need .mjs or "type": "module"

interview.q: How do you pass command line arguments to a Node script?
interview.a: Run node app.js a b --flag. They appear in process.argv; index 0 is the node binary, index 1 is the script path and the rest are your arguments. For flags use util.parseArgs.

interview.q: What is the REPL?
interview.a: The Read-Eval-Print Loop, an interactive shell started by running node with no file. It evaluates JavaScript line by line and is useful for quick experiments.

topics.title: npm Basics
topics.summary: npm installs, updates and publishes packages; know install, uninstall, update, ci and the lock file.
topics.description:
**npm** (Node Package Manager) is installed with Node. It downloads packages from the npm registry into `node_modules` and records them in `package.json`.

### Everyday commands
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm init -y` | Create a `package.json` with defaults |
| `npm install express` (`npm i`) | Add a dependency |
| `npm i -D vitest` | Add a **dev** dependency |
| `npm i -g pkg` | Install globally (CLI tools) |
| `npm uninstall pkg` | Remove a package |
| `npm update` | Update within allowed semver ranges |
| `npm outdated` | Show newer versions |
| `npm ls` | Show the dependency tree |
| `npm ci` | Clean, exact install from the lock file (CI and Docker) |
| `npm audit` | Check for known vulnerabilities |

### dependencies vs devDependencies
* `dependencies`: needed at runtime (express, mongoose)
* `devDependencies`: only for development (eslint, vitest, nodemon)
* `npm i --omit=dev` installs only production dependencies

### The lock file
`package-lock.json` records the **exact** version of every package in the tree. Commit it so every teammate and server installs identical code. Use `npm ci` in automation because it fails if the lock file and `package.json` disagree.

### Alternatives
**pnpm** (fast, disk efficient) and **Yarn** do the same job; **Bun** and **Deno** bring their own tools. The concepts are identical.
keyPoints: npm install adds to package.json and node_modules
Use -D for tooling, regular install for runtime packages
Commit package-lock.json; use npm ci in CI and Docker
npm audit checks for known vulnerabilities
pitfalls: Committing node_modules to git
Using npm install instead of npm ci in pipelines, which may change the lock file
Installing a package globally when a local dev dependency would do

examples.code:

interview.q: Difference between npm install and npm ci?
interview.a: npm install resolves versions and may update the lock file. npm ci deletes node_modules and installs exactly what the lock file says, failing if it does not match package.json, which makes it fast and reproducible for CI.

interview.q: Why commit package-lock.json?
interview.a: It pins every transitive dependency to an exact version and checksum so builds are reproducible and protected from surprise upgrades.

topics.title: package.json Explained
topics.summary: package.json is the manifest of a Node project: name, version, entry point, scripts, dependencies and module type.
topics.description:
Every Node project has a `package.json`. It describes the project and tells npm what to install.

### Important fields
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name`, `version` | Identity (needed to publish) |
| `description`, `license`, `author` | Metadata |
| `main` | Entry file for `require('pkg')` |
| `type` | `"module"` makes `.js` files ES modules; `"commonjs"` (default) keeps CommonJS |
| `exports` | Modern, strict map of what a package exposes |
| `scripts` | Named commands run by `npm run` |
| `dependencies` | Runtime packages |
| `devDependencies` | Development only |
| `peerDependencies` | Packages the host app must provide (plugins) |
| `engines` | Required Node/npm versions |
| `bin` | Command names for CLI packages |
| `files` | What gets published |
| `private: true` | Prevents accidental publishing |

### Version ranges
`"express": "^4.19.2"` means "any compatible 4.x.x at or above 4.19.2". See the semver topic for details.

### Typical app manifest
Most applications set `"private": true`, `"type": "module"`, a `start` and a `dev` script and an `engines` field.

### Tip
Edit `package.json` by hand freely, but use `npm install` to change dependencies so the lock file stays in sync.

type decides whether .js files are ESM or CommonJS
scripts define reusable commands, dependencies define installs
private: true avoids accidental publishing
engines documents the required Node version
pitfalls: Trailing commas or comments: package.json must be strict JSON
Putting build tools in dependencies and bloating production installs

examples.explanation: start, dev and test cover the daily workflow.

interview.q: What does the type field do?
interview.a: "type": "module" tells Node to treat .js files in that package as ES modules (import/export). Without it (or with "commonjs") .js files use require/module.exports. .mjs and .cjs always force a mode.

interview.q: dependencies vs devDependencies vs peerDependencies?
interview.a: dependencies are needed at runtime; devDependencies only while developing/building/testing; peerDependencies declare that the consuming app must supply a compatible version, typical for plugins and libraries.

topics.title: npm Scripts
topics.summary: The scripts field turns long commands into short names and supports pre/post hooks and local binaries.
topics.description:
The `scripts` section maps names to shell commands. Run one with `npm run <name>`. Four names are special and need no `run`: `npm start`, `npm test`, `npm stop` and `npm restart`.

### Why use scripts
* Short, memorable commands for the whole team
* They add `node_modules/.bin` to the PATH, so locally installed tools (eslint, vitest) work without a global install
* Same commands in your terminal and in CI

### Hooks
For any script `x`, `prex` runs before it and `postx` after it. `npm run build` first runs `prebuild`. Special lifecycle hooks: `prepare` (after install, used by Husky) and `prepublishOnly`.

### Passing arguments
Use `--` to forward arguments: `npm run dev -- --port 4000` ends up as `--port 4000` for the script.

### Chaining
* `a && b` runs b only if a succeeds
* `a ; b` runs both (not on Windows cmd)
* Packages such as `npm-run-all2` or `concurrently` run scripts in parallel
* `npm run build --workspaces` runs across a monorepo

### Environment variables
Set variables with `cross-env NODE_ENV=production node app.js` for Windows compatibility, or use `node --env-file`.

### Useful extras
`npm run` lists all scripts. Inside scripts, `npm_package_name` and `npm_package_version` are available as env vars.
keyPoints: Scripts are named shell commands run with npm run name
start and test can be run as npm start / npm test
node_modules/.bin is on the PATH inside scripts
pre and post prefixes create hooks, -- forwards arguments
pitfalls: Writing shell syntax that breaks on Windows (use cross-platform tools)
Forgetting the -- when forwarding flags to the underlying command

examples.explanation: npm run build runs prebuild, build, postbuild in order.

interview.q: How do you pass flags to an npm script?
interview.a: Put -- before them: npm run dev -- --port 4000. Everything after -- is appended to the script's command.

interview.q: Why can scripts run tools that are not installed globally?
interview.a: npm prepends node_modules/.bin to PATH while running scripts, so locally installed executables are found automatically.

topics.title: Semantic Versioning
topics.summary: Versions look like MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; the ^ and ~ symbols control which updates npm accepts.
topics.description:
npm packages follow **semver**: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, for example `4.18.2`.

* **PATCH** (4.18.**3**): bug fixes, nothing breaks
* **MINOR** (4.**19**.0): new backwards-compatible features
* **MAJOR** (**5**.0.0): breaking changes

### Range symbols in package.json
| Range | Accepts | Example result |
|---|---|---|
| `4.18.2` | exactly this version | 4.18.2 |
| `^4.18.2` | same major, at or above | 4.18.2 up to < 5.0.0 |
| `~4.18.2` | same minor, at or above | 4.18.2 up to < 4.19.0 |
| `>=4 <6` | explicit range | 4.x or 5.x |
| `*` or `latest` | anything | dangerous |

### Special case: 0.x versions
For `^0.2.3` only patch updates are accepted (`< 0.3.0`) because 0.x is considered unstable.

### Pre-releases
`2.0.0-beta.1` sorts before `2.0.0`. Tags such as `next` or `beta` are used for early access: `npm i pkg@beta`.

### Why it matters
`^` gives you automatic bug fixes, but the lock file is what actually stops surprise upgrades. Updating a **major** version requires reading the changelog.

### Checking
`npm outdated` shows current, wanted (within range) and latest versions. `npm view express versions` lists all.
keyPoints: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking.feature.fix
^ allows minor and patch updates, ~ allows only patch
Caret on 0.x versions behaves more strictly
The lock file freezes the exact versions that were installed
pitfalls: Assuming minor updates can never break anything (maintainers make mistakes)
Using * or latest in dependencies

interview.q: What does ^ mean in package.json?
interview.a: Accept any version that does not change the left-most non-zero digit. ^1.2.3 means >=1.2.3 <2.0.0, ^0.2.3 means >=0.2.3 <0.3.0.

interview.q: When does a package bump the major version?
interview.a: When it makes a backwards-incompatible change such as removing or renaming an API, so consumers must opt in and review the migration notes.

topics.title: npx and Running Package Binaries
topics.summary: npx runs a package's command without a global install, perfect for scaffolding tools and one-off scripts.
topics.description:
**npx** ships with npm. It runs a command from a package, using the local `node_modules/.bin` if the package is installed there, or downloading it temporarily if not.

### Common uses
* **Scaffolding**: `npx create-vite@latest my-app`, `npx create-next-app`
* **One-off tools**: `npx kill-port 3000`, `npx serve .`
* **Using a local binary**: `npx eslint .` after `npm i -D eslint`
* **Trying a specific version**: `npx typescript@5.4 --version`

### How it decides
1. Look in the local project's `node_modules/.bin`
2. Look in the PATH
3. Otherwise download into a cache and run it (npx asks first for unknown packages)

### Flags
* `-y` or `--yes` skip the install prompt (useful in CI)
* `-p pkg1 -p pkg2 command` use several packages
* `--no-install` fail instead of downloading

### Related tools
* `npm exec` is the underlying command
* `npm create vite@latest` is shorthand for `npx create-vite@latest`
* `pnpm dlx` and `yarn dlx` do the same in other managers

### Security note
Running `npx some-package` executes code from the internet with your permissions. Check the package name (typos are used by attackers) and prefer well known packages.
keyPoints: npx executes a package binary without a permanent install
It prefers local binaries over downloads
Great for scaffolding with create-* packages
Only run packages you trust: it executes arbitrary code
pitfalls: Typo-squatting: npx create-raect-app may be malicious
Forgetting @latest and scaffolding from a cached old version

examples.explanation: The first two download the tool on demand; the last uses your local install.

interview.q: What is the difference between npm install -g and npx?
interview.a: A global install keeps a permanent, possibly outdated copy on your machine. npx runs the package on demand (cached, or the local version), so you always control the version and avoid polluting global space.

interview.q: What is npm exec?
interview.a: The npm command that npx is built on. It runs a binary from a local or remote package, with npx being its convenient front end.

topics.title: node_modules and Dependency Resolution
topics.summary: node_modules holds installed packages in a nested tree; learn how lookup works, why it gets huge and how to manage it.
topics.description:
`node_modules` is the folder where npm places every package your project depends on, including the dependencies of your dependencies (**transitive** dependencies).

### How lookup works
When you write `require('lodash')` or `import 'lodash'`, Node looks in:
1. `./node_modules/lodash`
2. `../node_modules/lodash`
3. `../../node_modules/lodash` ... up to the filesystem root

This is why a package installed in the parent folder is visible to child folders.

### Flat tree and duplicates
npm tries to **hoist** (flatten) shared packages to the top level to avoid duplication. If two packages need incompatible versions, one is nested inside the other's own `node_modules`.

### Why it is heavy
A simple app can pull in hundreds of packages. This is the reason for:
* `.gitignore` containing `node_modules/`
* pnpm, which stores one copy globally and links it
* Docker layers that install dependencies before copying source

### Cleaning up
* Delete `node_modules` and run `npm ci` to fix strange errors
* `npm dedupe` merges duplicates, `npm prune` removes extraneous packages
* `npm ls package-name` shows who depends on a package and which version
* `npm explain pkg` explains why a package is installed

### Never edit inside
Changes in `node_modules` are lost on the next install. Use `patch-package` or fork the library if you need a fix.
keyPoints: node_modules contains direct and transitive dependencies
Node walks up parent folders to find a package
npm hoists shared versions, nesting only when versions conflict
Never commit it, never edit it; reinstall with npm ci
pitfalls: Committing node_modules to version control
Hand-editing a library inside node_modules
Copying node_modules between operating systems (native modules break)

interview.q: How does Node find a package imported by name?
interview.a: It looks for node_modules/<name> in the current file's directory, then each parent directory in turn up to the root, and uses the package's main or exports entry.

interview.q: Why is node_modules in .gitignore?
interview.a: It is large, reproducible from package.json plus the lock file, and may contain OS-specific binaries, so only the manifest and lock file are committed.

topics.title: Global Objects and Variables
topics.summary: globalThis, process, console, Buffer, timers, URL, fetch and module-scoped variables like __dirname.
topics.description:
Node exposes a set of **globals** that need no import.

### True globals
| Name | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `globalThis` | The global object (works everywhere, replaces `global` / `window`) |
| `process` | Info and control of the running process |
| `console` | Logging |
| `Buffer` | Binary data |
| `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate`, `queueMicrotask` | Scheduling |
| `URL`, `URLSearchParams`, `TextEncoder`, `TextDecoder` | Web standard utilities |
| `fetch`, `Request`, `Response`, `Headers`, `FormData` | HTTP client (undici) |
| `AbortController`, `structuredClone`, `performance`, `crypto` (Web Crypto) | Modern web APIs |

### Module-scoped variables (CommonJS only)
Each CommonJS file is wrapped in a function, so `require`, `module`, `exports`, `__filename` and `__dirname` are **local to the file**, not real globals.

### ES module equivalents
ESM has no `__dirname`. Use:
* `import.meta.url` (file URL of the current module)
* `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` (Node 20.11+)
* `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)` for older versions

### Variables declared at the top level
`var x = 1` in a Node file does **not** create `globalThis.x`, because the file is a module with its own scope. This differs from browser scripts.

### Avoid polluting globals
Assigning `globalThis.config = ...` makes hidden dependencies and bugs. Export from a module instead.
keyPoints: globalThis is the universal global object in Node and browsers
process, Buffer, console, timers, fetch and URL are available without imports
__dirname and __filename exist only in CommonJS; ESM uses import.meta.dirname
Top-level var does not create a global in Node

Storing shared state on globalThis

interview.q: Are __dirname and require globals?
interview.a: No. In CommonJS every file is wrapped in a function that receives exports, require, module, __filename and __dirname as parameters, so they are module-scoped. ES modules do not have them.

interview.q: What is globalThis?
interview.a: A standard reference to the global object that works in every JS environment (window in browsers, global in Node, self in workers).

topics.title: CommonJS vs ES Modules
topics.summary: require/module.exports versus import/export: syntax, loading behaviour, interop and how to choose.
topics.description:
Node supports two module systems.

| | CommonJS (CJS) | ES Modules (ESM) |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | `require()`, `module.exports` | `import`, `export` |
| Loading | Synchronous | Asynchronous, statically analysed |
| File types | `.js` (default), `.cjs` | `.mjs`, or `.js` with `"type": "module"` |
| Top-level `await` | No | Yes |
| `__dirname` | Yes | No (use `import.meta.dirname`) |
| Strict mode | Optional | Always |
| Live bindings | Copies of values | Live read-only views |

### Enabling ESM
Put `"type": "module"` in `package.json`, or name files `.mjs`.

### Interop rules
* ESM can `import` CommonJS (module.exports becomes the default export)
* CommonJS `require()` of an ES module is supported in current Node versions (22.12+ and 24) when the module has no top-level `await`; before that you needed `await import()`
* Dynamic `import('./x.js')` works in both systems and returns a promise

### Which should you pick?
New projects: **ESM**. It is the language standard, supports top-level await and tree shaking, and is what browsers use. CommonJS remains everywhere in older code and docs, so you must read both.

### Named vs default
CJS: `module.exports = { add }`. ESM: `export function add() {}` or `export default`. Mixing `module.exports` and `export` in one file is an error.

### Import specifiers
ESM requires the **file extension** for relative imports (`./utils.js`), unlike many bundlers. Built-ins use the `node:` prefix: `import fs from 'node:fs'`.
keyPoints: CJS: require and module.exports, synchronous; ESM: import and export, async and static
Enable ESM with "type": "module" or the .mjs extension
ESM needs file extensions in relative imports and has no __dirname
Use dynamic import() to load ESM from CJS (or require(esm) on new Node)
Prefer ESM for new code
pitfalls: Forgetting the .js extension in a relative ESM import
Using require in a "type": "module" package (ReferenceError)
Mixing module.exports and export in one file

interview.q: require vs import: key differences?
interview.a: require is a synchronous function evaluated at runtime and returns a copy of module.exports. import is static syntax, resolved before execution, asynchronous, gives live bindings and enables tree shaking and top-level await.

interview.q: How do you use __dirname in ESM?

topics.title: Module Resolution and Caching
topics.summary: How Node resolves relative paths, node_modules names, index files and exports maps, and why modules are cached.
topics.description:
### Resolution order for `require(x)`
1. **Core module** (`fs`, `node:path`) always wins
2. **Relative or absolute path** (`./a`, `../a`, `/a`): try the exact file, then add `.js`, `.json`, `.node`; then treat it as a directory (`package.json` `main`, then `index.js`)
3. **Bare name** (`lodash`): walk up through every `node_modules` folder

`require.resolve('x')` prints the file that would be loaded without running it.

### The exports map
Modern packages use `"exports"` in `package.json` to declare their public entry points. Anything not listed cannot be imported (deep imports like `pkg/lib/internal.js` throw `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`). It also allows conditions:

`{ "exports": { "import": "./esm/index.js", "require": "./cjs/index.cjs" } }`

### Caching
A module runs **once**. The result is stored in `require.cache` (CJS) or the module map (ESM); later imports get the same object. This makes modules natural **singletons** (a db connection, a config object).

### Circular dependencies
If `a` requires `b` and `b` requires `a`, `b` receives the **partially filled** `exports` of `a`. Symptoms: `undefined` imports. Fix by restructuring, moving shared code to a third module or requiring lazily inside functions.

### ESM differences
ESM does not search extensions or `index.js` for relative imports; you must write full paths. Use `import.meta.resolve()` to resolve a specifier.

### Aliases
Node supports `"imports": { "#utils/*": "./src/utils/*.js" }` for private aliases starting with `#`.

interview.q: Why does requiring the same module twice not re-run it?
interview.a: Node caches the module by resolved filename in require.cache after the first load, so later require calls return the cached exports. This makes modules behave like singletons.

interview.q: What is the package.json exports field for?
interview.a: It defines a package's public API: the only paths consumers may import, optionally per condition (import, require, node, default), which prevents deep imports into internals.

topics.description:
Node ships a standard library. You never install these; just import them with the **`node:` prefix** (clear, and avoids clashing with npm packages of the same name).

### Map of the important ones
| Area | Modules |
|---|---|
| Files and paths | `fs`, `fs/promises`, `path`, `os`, `url` |
| Network | `http`, `https`, `http2`, `net`, `dgram`, `dns`, `tls` |
| Async tools | `events`, `stream`, `stream/promises`, `timers/promises`, `async_hooks` |
| Data | `buffer`, `zlib`, `string_decoder`, `querystring` |
| Security | `crypto` |
| Processes and threads | `child_process`, `cluster`, `worker_threads`, `process` |
| Utilities | `util`, `assert`, `readline`, `perf_hooks`, `diagnostics_channel` |
| Testing and storage | `test` (`node:test`), `sqlite` (`node:sqlite`) |
| Diagnostics | `inspector`, `v8`, `repl`, `trace_events` |

### How to import
CommonJS: `const fs = require('node:fs');`
ESM: `import fs from 'node:fs';` or named: `import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';`

### Promise versions
Many callback APIs have promise twins: `node:fs/promises`, `node:timers/promises`, `node:dns/promises`, `node:readline/promises`, `node:stream/promises`. Prefer them with `async/await`.

### Discover more
In the REPL, `require('node:module').builtinModules` lists all of them. The official docs at nodejs.org/api document each module with stability markers (Stable, Experimental, Deprecated).

### Stability index
Check the stability badge: *Experimental* APIs can change in any release. Avoid them in critical production code unless you pin the Node version.

topics.title: fs: Reading and Writing Files
topics.summary: The fs module offers synchronous, callback and promise APIs; prefer fs/promises in application code.
topics.description:
The **`fs`** module talks to the file system. Every operation comes in three styles.

| Style | Example | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronous | `fs.readFileSync(p, 'utf8')` | Start-up scripts, CLIs, config loading |
| Callback | `fs.readFile(p, 'utf8', cb)` | Legacy code |
| Promise | `await fs.promises.readFile(p, 'utf8')` | Servers and everything modern |

Import the promise version with `import fs from 'node:fs/promises'`.

### Common operations
* `readFile`, `writeFile` (overwrites), `appendFile`
* `copyFile`, `rename`, `unlink` (delete a file), `rm` (delete files or folders)
* `access`, `stat` to check existence, size and type
* Without an encoding, `readFile` returns a **Buffer**; pass `'utf8'` to get a string

### Why not sync in a server?
Sync calls block the event loop: while one request waits for the disk, every other request freezes. Use them only before the server starts listening.

### Errors
Failures throw errors with a `code` such as `ENOENT` (not found), `EACCES` (permission), `EEXIST` or `EISDIR`. Always handle them:
`try { ... } catch (err) { if (err.code === 'ENOENT') ... }`

### Checking existence
Avoid `exists` followed by read (race condition). Just try the operation and handle `ENOENT`.

### Large files
`readFile` loads the whole file into memory. For big files use streams (see the streams topic) so memory stays flat.

### Paths
Relative paths are resolved against `process.cwd()`, not the file's location. Build absolute paths with `path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'file.txt')`.

interview.a: It blocks the single JavaScript thread until the disk read finishes, so no other request can be handled meanwhile. Use fs.promises (non-blocking) inside handlers; sync calls are fine at start-up.

interview.q: How do you check whether a file exists?
interview.a: Prefer to try the operation and catch ENOENT, because checking first with exists/access can race with other processes. fs.access or fs.stat in a try/catch also works when you only need the check.

topics.title: fs: Directories, Streams and Watching
topics.summary: List and create folders, walk trees recursively, stream big files and react to changes with fs.watch.
topics.description:
### Directories
* `fs.mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })` creates nested folders and does not fail if they exist
* `fs.readdir(dir)` returns names; `{ withFileTypes: true }` returns `Dirent` objects with `isFile()` and `isDirectory()`
* `fs.readdir(dir, { recursive: true })` lists the whole tree (Node 20+)
* `fs.rm(path, { recursive: true, force: true })` is `rm -rf`
* `fs.mkdtemp(prefix)` makes a unique temporary folder
* `fs.glob(pattern)` finds files by pattern in current Node versions

### Metadata
`fs.stat` gives `size`, `mtime`, `birthtime`, `mode`, `isFile()`, `isDirectory()`. `fs.lstat` does not follow symlinks.

### Streams for big files
`fs.createReadStream(file)` and `fs.createWriteStream(file)` move data in 64 KB chunks, so memory usage stays small. Combine with `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises` to copy or transform (compress, parse) safely.

### Watching for changes
`fs.watch(path)` emits events when a file or folder changes. It is the foundation of `node --watch`, nodemon and dev servers. Behaviour differs per OS (duplicate events are common), so debounce them. In ESM you can iterate: `for await (const e of fs.promises.watch(dir))`.

### File handles
`const fh = await fs.open(path, 'r+')` gives low-level control (read at an offset, write at a position). Always `await fh.close()` in a `finally` block, or use `await using` where available.

### Permissions
`fs.chmod`, `fs.access(path, fs.constants.R_OK)` check/set permission bits (mostly meaningful on Linux and macOS).

interview.a: Editors and operating systems emit several low-level events (truncate then write, temp file then rename) for one save. Debounce events for a few milliseconds and compare file contents or mtime.

topics.title: path Module
topics.summary: Build, parse and normalise file paths in a cross-platform way with path.join, resolve, basename, extname and friends.
topics.description:
Never build paths by string concatenation (`dir + '/' + file`). Windows uses `\` and Linux/macOS use `/`. The **`path`** module handles the difference for you.

### Most used functions
| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `path.join(...parts)` | Join and normalise segments |
| `path.resolve(...parts)` | Produce an **absolute** path, processing right to left until one is absolute; starts from `process.cwd()` |
| `path.basename(p, ext?)` | Last part (file name) |
| `path.dirname(p)` | Folder part |
| `path.extname(p)` | Extension including the dot |
| `path.parse(p)` / `path.format(obj)` | Split into `{ root, dir, base, name, ext }` and back |
| `path.normalize(p)` | Collapse `..`, `.` and double slashes |
| `path.relative(from, to)` | Relative path between two places |
| `path.isAbsolute(p)` | Boolean |
| `path.sep`, `path.delimiter` | `/` or `\`, and `:` or `;` |

### join vs resolve
* `join` simply glues and cleans: `join('a', 'b')` is `a/b`
* `resolve` always returns an absolute path: `resolve('a', 'b')` is `<cwd>/a/b`

### posix and win32
`path.posix` and `path.win32` force one style regardless of the OS. Use `path.posix` for URLs and archive paths.

### Security: path traversal
When joining user input to a base folder, a value like `../../etc/passwd` can escape it. After resolving, check that the result still starts with the base folder.

topics.title: os Module
topics.summary: Read information about the machine: CPUs, memory, platform, hostname, home and temp directories.
topics.description:
The **`os`** module exposes details about the operating system and hardware. It is useful for diagnostics, choosing worker counts and writing cross-platform tools.

### Frequent members
| Member | Returns |
|---|---|
| `os.platform()` | `'linux'`, `'darwin'`, `'win32'` |
| `os.arch()` | `'x64'`, `'arm64'` |
| `os.cpus()` | Array with one entry per logical core |
| `os.availableParallelism()` | Number of threads you should use (respects container limits better than `cpus().length`) |
| `os.totalmem()` / `os.freemem()` | Memory in bytes |
| `os.homedir()` | User home directory |
| `os.tmpdir()` | Temp directory |
| `os.hostname()` | Machine name |
| `os.uptime()` | Seconds since boot |
| `os.loadavg()` | 1, 5 and 15 minute load (always zeros on Windows) |
| `os.networkInterfaces()` | IP addresses |
| `os.EOL` | Line ending: `\n` or `\r\n` |
| `os.userInfo()` | Current user |

### When to use
* Sizing a `cluster` or worker pool: `os.availableParallelism()`
* Storing cache files: `path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'myapp')`
* Platform specific behaviour: `if (os.platform() === 'win32') ...`
* Health endpoints that report free memory

### Containers note
Inside Docker or Kubernetes, `os.totalmem()` returns the **host** memory, not the container limit. Use `process.constrainedMemory()` or read the cgroup files for real limits.

topics.title: URL and URLSearchParams
topics.summary: Parse, build and modify URLs and query strings safely with the WHATWG URL classes.
topics.description:
Do not split URLs with regular expressions. Use the standard **`URL`** and **`URLSearchParams`** classes (global in Node, same as in browsers).

### Parsing
`new URL('https://user:pw@example.com:8080/a/b?x=1#top')` gives:
* `protocol` `https:`, `host` `example.com:8080`, `hostname`, `port`
* `pathname` `/a/b`, `search` `?x=1`, `hash` `#top`
* `origin`, `href`, `username`, `password`

An invalid URL throws `TypeError` (`ERR_INVALID_URL`), so wrap user input in try/catch. `URL.canParse(str)` checks without throwing.

### Relative URLs
`new URL('../img/a.png', 'https://site.com/blog/post/')` resolves against a base.

### Query strings
`url.searchParams` is a live `URLSearchParams`:
* `get`, `getAll`, `has`, `append`, `set`, `delete`
* Iterable: `for (const [k, v] of params)`
* `toString()` encodes spaces as `+` and special characters safely
* `Object.fromEntries(params)` converts to a plain object (last duplicate wins)

### In an HTTP server
`req.url` is just the path and query (`/search?q=node`). Combine with a base to parse: `new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost')`.

### File URLs
`import.meta.url` is a `file://` URL. Convert with `fileURLToPath(url)` and `pathToFileURL(path)` from `node:url`.

### Legacy API
`url.parse()` and the `querystring` module are legacy. Avoid them for new code.

topics.summary: util bundles helpers: promisify callback APIs, deep-print objects, parse CLI flags, format strings and check types.
topics.description:
The **`util`** module is a toolbox of small helpers.

### util.promisify
Turns an error-first callback function into one that returns a promise:
`const sleep = util.promisify(setTimeout)`. Many core APIs already have promise versions, but older libraries do not.
Opposite: `util.callbackify`.

### util.inspect
What `console.log` uses internally. Options: `depth` (default 2, `null` = unlimited), `colors`, `compact`, `breakLength`, `showHidden`. Define `[util.inspect.custom]` on a class to control how it prints. `console.dir(obj, { depth: null })` is the shortcut.

### util.parseArgs
Parses command line arguments without a dependency (stable since Node 20). Declare `options` with `type` (`string` or `boolean`), `short` aliases, `default` and `multiple`. Positional arguments need `allowPositionals: true`.

### util.format
printf-style formatting: `%s` string, `%d` number, `%i` integer, `%j` JSON, `%o`/`%O` objects, `%%` percent.

### util.styleText
Adds terminal colours without a library: `util.styleText('green', 'OK')`.

### util.types and util.isDeepStrictEqual
`util.types.isPromise(x)`, `isRegExp`, `isDate`. `util.isDeepStrictEqual(a, b)` compares objects by value.

### util.deprecate
Wrap an old function to print a one-time warning when it is called.

### util.TextEncoder / TextDecoder
Convert strings to UTF-8 bytes and back.

### util.debuglog
Logs only when `NODE_DEBUG=name` is set, ideal for library diagnostics.

topics.title: events: EventEmitter
topics.summary: The observer pattern at the heart of Node: on, once, emit, error events and the memory leak warning.
topics.description:
Much of Node (streams, servers, processes) is built on **`EventEmitter`**. An emitter lets objects announce that something happened and lets other code react.

### Core API
* `emitter.on(name, listener)` (alias `addListener`) subscribes
* `emitter.once(name, listener)` runs only the first time
* `emitter.emit(name, ...args)` calls all listeners **synchronously**, in the order they were added, and returns `true` if there were any
* `emitter.off(name, listener)` / `removeAllListeners(name)` unsubscribes
* `emitter.prependListener` runs a listener first
* `listenerCount(name)`, `eventNames()`

### The special `'error'` event
If an emitter emits `'error'` and **no listener** exists, Node throws and the process crashes. Always attach an error listener to emitters you create (streams, sockets).

### Making your own emitter
Extend the class: `class Chat extends EventEmitter {}`. This is how you build decoupled modules such as job queues, loggers or game engines.

### Waiting for an event
`await once(emitter, 'ready')` (from `node:events`) turns an event into a promise. `on(emitter, 'data')` gives an async iterator.

### Memory leak warning
More than 10 listeners for one event prints `MaxListenersExceededWarning`. It usually means you add listeners inside a loop or request handler without removing them. Raise it with `setMaxListeners` only when it is intentional.

### Sync vs async
`emit` is synchronous. If a listener is slow it blocks the emitter. Use `setImmediate` or queue work inside the listener for heavy tasks.

### EventTarget
Browsers use `EventTarget` and `addEventListener`; Node supports it too, but EventEmitter remains the standard in Node APIs.

topics.title: Buffer and Binary Data
topics.summary: Buffers hold raw bytes; learn creation, encodings (utf8, hex, base64), slicing and when you meet them.
topics.description:
A **Buffer** is a fixed-size chunk of memory holding raw bytes. It is a subclass of `Uint8Array` and is used for files, network packets, images, encryption and anything that is not plain text.

### Creating buffers
* `Buffer.from('hello')` from a string (UTF-8 by default)
* `Buffer.from([104, 105])` from bytes
* `Buffer.from(str, 'base64' | 'hex')` decoding
* `Buffer.alloc(10)` zero-filled, **safe**
* `Buffer.allocUnsafe(10)` faster, may contain old memory (never send it to clients unless fully overwritten)
* `Buffer.concat([a, b])`

### Converting
`buf.toString('utf8' | 'hex' | 'base64' | 'base64url')`. Example: `Buffer.from('hello').toString('base64')` is `aGVsbG8=`.

### Length is bytes, not characters
`'héllo'.length` is 5 but `Buffer.from('héllo').length` is 6, because `é` takes two bytes in UTF-8. Remember this for `Content-Length` headers and limits.

### Reading and writing numbers
`buf.readUInt32BE(0)`, `buf.writeInt16LE(-2, 4)`; BE/LE is big or little endian. Used when speaking binary protocols.

### Other helpers
* `buf.slice` / `subarray` share memory with the original (no copy)
* `buf.equals(other)`, `Buffer.compare`, `buf.indexOf`
* `Buffer.byteLength(str)` counts bytes without allocating
* Indexing `buf[0]` gives a byte (0-255)

### Where you meet them
`fs.readFile` without an encoding, stream `data` events, `crypto` outputs, and HTTP request bodies.

topics.title: crypto: Hashing, HMAC and Random Values
topics.summary: Create hashes, HMAC signatures, random tokens, UUIDs and encrypt data; know when to use bcrypt or argon2 instead.
topics.description:
The **`crypto`** module wraps OpenSSL for security tasks.

### Hashing
`crypto.createHash('sha256').update(data).digest('hex')`. A hash is one-way and always gives the same output for the same input. Use SHA-256 or SHA-512 for checksums and fingerprints. **MD5 and SHA-1 are broken** for security.

### HMAC
`crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(data).digest('hex')` produces a hash that also proves the sender knew the **secret key**. It is used for webhook signatures, signed cookies and JWT HS256. Compare signatures with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` to avoid timing attacks.

### Random values
* `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')` for tokens, secrets and salts
* `crypto.randomUUID()` for a v4 UUID
* `crypto.randomInt(1, 100)` for an unbiased random integer
* **Never** use `Math.random()` for anything security related

### Passwords
Plain hashes are too fast for passwords. Use a slow, salted algorithm:
* Built in: `crypto.scrypt` / `scryptSync(password, salt, 64)`
* Libraries: **bcrypt** or **argon2** (best choice today)

### Encryption
Symmetric: `createCipheriv('aes-256-gcm', key, iv)` (use a fresh 12-byte IV per message and store the auth tag). Asymmetric: `generateKeyPairSync('rsa' | 'ed25519')`, `sign`, `verify`.

### Web Crypto
`globalThis.crypto.subtle` offers the browser-compatible API, and `crypto.getRandomValues` works everywhere.

topics.title: zlib: Compression
topics.summary: Compress and decompress data with gzip, deflate and brotli, in memory or as streams.
topics.description:
**`zlib`** compresses data using gzip, deflate or brotli. Compression saves bandwidth and disk space, especially for text (JSON, HTML, logs) which often shrinks by 70-90%.

### Three APIs
1. **Sync**: `zlib.gzipSync(buf)` / `gunzipSync` for small data
2. **Async/callback** or promisified: `gzip(buf, cb)`
3. **Streams**: `zlib.createGzip()` / `createGunzip()` for large files and HTTP

### Algorithms
| Format | Functions | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| gzip | `gzip`, `gunzip` | Most common (files, HTTP) |
| deflate | `deflate`, `inflate` | Raw zlib format |
| brotli | `brotliCompress`, `brotliDecompress` | Better ratio, standard for HTTPS text |

### Streaming a file
`pipeline(createReadStream('big.log'), createGzip(), createWriteStream('big.log.gz'))` keeps memory constant.

### HTTP compression
Browsers send `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br`. A server can compress responses and add `Content-Encoding: gzip`. In real apps use the `compression` middleware or let nginx/CDN do it.

### Levels
`{ level: 9 }` is smallest but slowest; `level: 1` is fastest. Default (6) is a good balance.

### Security: zip bombs
A tiny input can expand to gigabytes. When decompressing untrusted data set `maxOutputLength`.

### CPU note
Compression is CPU-intensive. Sync versions block the event loop; the async ones use the thread pool.

interview.a: Check the Accept-Encoding header, pipe the response body through zlib.createGzip() (or brotli), and set Content-Encoding. Usually the compression middleware or a reverse proxy does this.

interview.q: Why is the sync zlib API risky on servers?
interview.a: It runs on the main thread, blocking the event loop during compression. The async and stream APIs run on the libuv thread pool.

topics.title: child_process
topics.summary: Run shell commands and other programs from Node with exec, execFile, spawn and fork.
topics.description:
**`child_process`** starts other programs from your script (git, ffmpeg, python, another Node file).

| Function | Best for | Output |
|---|---|---|
| `exec(cmd, cb)` | Short shell commands, small output | Buffered string |
| `execFile(file, args, cb)` | Run a program **without a shell** (safer) | Buffered |
| `spawn(cmd, args)` | Long running or large output | Streams (`stdout`, `stderr`) |
| `fork(modulePath)` | Another **Node** script with an IPC message channel | `send()` / `on('message')` |
| `execSync`, `spawnSync` | Scripts and build tools | Blocking |

### Promises
`const { promisify } = require('node:util'); const execP = promisify(exec);` returns `{ stdout, stderr }`.

### spawn in detail
`const child = spawn('ls', ['-la'])` gives `child.stdout.on('data', ...)`, `child.on('close', code => ...)` and `child.kill()`. Options: `cwd`, `env`, `stdio: 'inherit'` (pass through to your terminal), `shell: true`.

### Exit codes and errors
A non-zero exit code is a failure. `'error'` fires if the program cannot start (not found). `exec` rejects with an error that has `code`, `stdout` and `stderr`.

### Security: command injection
Building a command string such as `"git log " + userInput` lets a user inject `; rm -rf /`. Never put untrusted data in a shell string. Use `execFile` or `spawn` with an arguments **array** and `shell: false`.

### fork vs worker_threads
`fork` creates a whole new process with its own memory (heavier, isolated). `worker_threads` shares the process and is lighter for CPU work.

interview.q: How do you avoid command injection?
interview.a: Never interpolate user input into a shell string. Use execFile or spawn with the program and an array of arguments, without shell: true, and validate input against an allow-list.

topics.title: readline: Interactive Input
topics.summary: Read user input line by line from the terminal or from a large file.
topics.description:
**`readline`** reads a stream one line at a time. It has two main jobs: interactive prompts in CLI tools and processing big text files line by line.

### Prompting the user
With `node:readline/promises`:
`const rl = readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin, output: process.stdout }); const name = await rl.question('Name? '); rl.close();`

Always call `rl.close()`, otherwise the process stays alive waiting for input.

### Reading a file line by line
`createInterface({ input: fs.createReadStream('big.csv'), crlfDelay: Infinity })` then `for await (const line of rl)`. Memory stays small even for huge files; this is the standard way to parse logs and CSV.

### Events
* `'line'` for each line
* `'close'` at the end of input or Ctrl+C / Ctrl+D
* `rl.on('SIGINT')` to customise Ctrl+C

### Other helpers
* `readline.clearLine`, `cursorTo`, `moveCursor` for progress bars
* `rl.setPrompt('> ')` and `rl.prompt()` build a REPL-like loop
* Piped input works: `echo "Ann" | node ask.mjs`

### For rich CLIs
Libraries such as `inquirer`, `prompts` and `@clack/prompts` add menus, checkboxes and validation on top of the same idea.

### Windows line endings
Use `crlfDelay: Infinity` so `\r\n` counts as a single line break.

topics.title: Timers: setTimeout, setImmediate, timers/promises
topics.summary: Schedule work with setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate and process.nextTick, and use the promise timers.
topics.description:
Node provides the familiar browser timers plus a few extras.

| API | Runs |
|---|---|
| `setTimeout(fn, ms)` | After at least `ms` milliseconds |
| `setInterval(fn, ms)` | Repeatedly every `ms` |
| `setImmediate(fn)` | After the current I/O phase (check phase of the event loop) |
| `process.nextTick(fn)` | Before anything else, right after the current operation |
| `queueMicrotask(fn)` | In the microtask queue (like promise callbacks) |

### Timer objects
In Node, `setTimeout` returns a `Timeout` object, not a number. Methods: `clearTimeout(t)`, `t.unref()` (do not keep the process alive for this timer), `t.ref()`, `t.refresh()`.

### Not exact
The delay is a **minimum**. If the event loop is busy the callback runs later. Never use timers for precise timing.

### Promise timers
`import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises'` gives `await sleep(1000)`, and supports an `AbortSignal`. `setInterval` there is an async iterator.

### Clearing
Always clear intervals you no longer need, or the process never exits. Using `unref()` on a background interval (metrics, cleanup) lets Node exit when real work is done.

### Zero delay
`setTimeout(fn, 0)` actually becomes 1 ms. Compared to `setImmediate`, the order is not guaranteed in the main module but is always immediate-first inside an I/O callback (see the event loop topic).

### Long delays
Delays above 2,147,483,647 ms (about 24.8 days) overflow and fire immediately.

interview.a: No. 100 ms is the minimum delay. The callback is queued once the time elapsed, but runs only when the event loop is free, so it can be late if other work is running.

interview.q: What does timer.unref() do?
interview.a: It tells Node not to wait for this timer before exiting. If only unref'd timers remain, the process ends. Useful for housekeeping tasks.

topics.title: assert and Validating Assumptions
topics.summary: node:assert provides strict equality, deep equality and throws checks used by tests and defensive code.
topics.description:
**`assert`** throws an `AssertionError` when a condition is false. It is the base of `node:test` and a good way to check assumptions in scripts.

### Use the strict mode
Import from `node:assert/strict` (or `assert.strict`). Then `equal` means `===` and `deepEqual` means strict deep comparison. The loose versions use `==` and cause surprising passes (`1 == '1'`).

### Main functions
| Function | Checks |
|---|---|
| `assert.ok(value)` / `assert(value)` | Truthy |
| `assert.equal(a, b)` | `a === b` (strict mode) |
| `assert.notEqual(a, b)` | Not equal |
| `assert.deepEqual(a, b)` | Objects/arrays equal by value |
| `assert.throws(fn, expected)` | `fn` throws a matching error |
| `assert.rejects(promiseOrFn, expected)` | Promise rejects |
| `assert.match(str, regex)` | String matches regex |
| `assert.fail(message)` | Always fails |

### Custom messages
Last argument: `assert.equal(total, 10, 'cart total should be 10')`. Without it Node prints a helpful diff of actual vs expected.

### Production use?
Use assert for **programmer errors** and invariants during tests and scripts. For validating user input, throw proper errors (400 responses); do not rely on assert, and avoid assert in hot paths.

### Test runner
`node --test` discovers files and runs `node:test`, which uses assert for the checks themselves. See the testing section.

interview.q: How do you assert that an async function fails?
interview.a: Use await assert.rejects(fnOrPromise, expectedError). Without await the assertion may not finish before the test ends.

topics.title: The process Object
topics.summary: process gives access to arguments, environment variables, exit codes, signals, stdin/stdout, memory and uptime.
topics.description:
**`process`** is a global object describing the current Node process.

### Information
* `process.argv`: `[nodePath, scriptPath, ...args]`
* `process.env`: environment variables (all values are strings)
* `process.cwd()`: current working directory; `process.chdir(dir)`
* `process.pid`, `process.platform`, `process.version`, `process.versions`
* `process.uptime()`, `process.memoryUsage()`, `process.cpuUsage()`, `process.hrtime.bigint()`

### Standard streams
`process.stdin`, `process.stdout`, `process.stderr` are streams. `console.log` writes to stdout and `console.error` to stderr. Pipes: `echo hi | node app.js` fills stdin.

### Exiting
* `process.exit(code)` stops immediately; pending async work is lost
* `process.exitCode = 1` sets the code and lets the process end naturally (preferred)
* Exit code 0 = success

### Events
* `'exit'` (sync cleanup only) and `'beforeExit'`
* `'uncaughtException'` and `'unhandledRejection'`: last-resort handlers: log and exit, do not continue
* **Signals**: `'SIGINT'` (Ctrl+C), `'SIGTERM'` (kill, Docker/Kubernetes stop). Handle them for graceful shutdown. (`SIGKILL` cannot be caught.)

### Environment variables
`process.env.PORT ?? 3000`. Values are strings so convert: `Number(process.env.PORT)`. Setting `process.env.X = undefined` stores the string `'undefined'`; use `delete`.

### nextTick
`process.nextTick(fn)` runs before promise microtasks (see the event loop).

### Warnings and loading env files
`process.loadEnvFile('.env')` loads a file at runtime, and `process.emitWarning()` raises warnings.

interview.a: SIGINT is sent by Ctrl+C, SIGTERM is the polite termination request used by Docker, Kubernetes and process managers. Handle both to close servers and database connections before exiting. SIGKILL cannot be handled.

topics.title: worker_threads
topics.summary: Run CPU-heavy JavaScript on separate threads without blocking the event loop, with message passing and shared memory.
topics.description:
Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, so a CPU-heavy loop freezes every request. **`worker_threads`** lets you run JavaScript in parallel **threads** inside the same process.

### Basics
* `new Worker(file, { workerData })` starts a worker
* In the worker: `parentPort.postMessage(result)` and `parentPort.on('message', ...)`
* `isMainThread` tells which side you are in, so one file can contain both
* Events on the worker: `'message'`, `'error'`, `'exit'`

### Communication
Messages are copied with the **structured clone** algorithm (objects, arrays, Maps, typed arrays). To avoid copying large data:
* **Transfer** ownership of an `ArrayBuffer`: `postMessage(buf, [buf])`
* Share memory with `SharedArrayBuffer` and coordinate using `Atomics`

### Workers vs child processes vs cluster
| | worker_threads | child_process / cluster |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | Same process, separate heaps | Separate processes |
| Start cost | Lower | Higher |
| Best for | CPU tasks (hashing, image resize, parsing) | Isolation, scaling servers on all cores |

### Not for I/O
Workers do not make database or HTTP calls faster; Node's async I/O is already non-blocking. Use workers only for CPU work.

### Worker pools
Creating a worker per request is expensive (tens of ms). Keep a pool and reuse workers. Libraries: **piscina**, **workerpool**.

### Memory limits
Each worker has its own V8 heap; set `resourceLimits: { maxOldGenerationSizeMb: 256 }`.

interview.q: How do workers share data?
interview.a: Via postMessage (data is cloned or ArrayBuffers transferred) or via SharedArrayBuffer plus Atomics for true shared memory.

topics.title: cluster
topics.summary: Fork one worker process per CPU core, all sharing the same server port, and restart them when they die.
topics.description:
A Node process uses only **one CPU core** for JavaScript. On an 8-core server you waste seven. The **`cluster`** module starts several copies (workers) of your app that all listen on the **same port**.

### How it works
1. The **primary** process (`cluster.isPrimary`) calls `cluster.fork()` once per core.
2. Each worker is a separate Node process with its own memory, event loop and V8.
3. The primary accepts connections and distributes them to workers (round-robin on Linux/macOS).
4. If a worker crashes, the primary can fork a new one.

### Example outline
`if (cluster.isPrimary) { for (...) cluster.fork(); cluster.on('exit', () => cluster.fork()); } else { http.createServer(...).listen(3000); }`

### Things to remember
* **No shared memory**: in-memory sessions, caches, counters and websockets are per worker. Use Redis or a database for shared state.
* Each worker has its own database connection pool: size pools accordingly.
* Workers communicate via IPC messages (`process.send`).
* Zero-downtime restarts: restart workers one at a time.

### In practice
Most teams do not write cluster code by hand:
* **PM2** has `pm2 start app.js -i max` (cluster mode)
* **Containers**: run one process per container and scale containers horizontally
* **Kubernetes** / load balancers do the distribution

### cluster vs worker_threads
cluster scales **request handling** across cores; worker_threads offloads **CPU tasks**.

interview.a: Workers do not share memory, so in-process state such as sessions, caches or WebSocket connections must move to external stores like Redis (or use sticky sessions).

topics.title: perf_hooks: Measuring Performance
topics.summary: Measure durations with performance.now, marks and measures, timerify functions and track event loop delay.
topics.description:
The **`perf_hooks`** module (and the global `performance`) gives high resolution timing.

### Quick timing
* `performance.now()` returns milliseconds with microsecond precision since the process started
* `console.time('label')` / `console.timeEnd('label')` is the casual version
* `process.hrtime.bigint()` returns nanoseconds as a BigInt
* `Date.now()` is not suitable for benchmarks because the system clock can jump

### Marks and measures
`performance.mark('start')`, `performance.mark('end')`, `performance.measure('task', 'start', 'end')` record named points and durations. Read them with `performance.getEntriesByName('task')`.

### PerformanceObserver
Listen to entries as they are created, including built-ins such as garbage collection (`'gc'`), HTTP requests, and `'function'` entries produced by `performance.timerify(fn)`.

### Event loop delay
`monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 20 })` creates a histogram showing how long the loop is blocked. Values (mean, p99, max) reveal blocking code. It is also a great health metric.

`performance.eventLoopUtilization()` returns how busy the loop is (0 to 1).

### When to use
* Compare two algorithm implementations
* Time database queries or external calls and log slow ones
* Expose event loop lag in monitoring dashboards

### Benchmark tips
Run code many times, warm up first (JIT), and use dedicated tools (`mitata`, `tinybench`) for serious comparisons.

topics.title: diagnostics_channel and Observability Hooks

topics.description:
**`diagnostics_channel`** is a lightweight, named publish/subscribe system. Libraries publish data on channels, and observability tools (APM, tracing, loggers) subscribe without patching the library.

### Why it exists
Before this, monitoring tools had to **monkey-patch** modules like `http` or `pg`. That is fragile. A channel offers an official, stable hook with almost zero cost when nobody subscribes.

### API
* `diagnostics_channel.channel('my.event')` get a channel object
* `channel.publish(data)` send a message
* `channel.subscribe((message, name) => ...)` / `unsubscribe`
* `channel.hasSubscribers` check before building expensive payloads
* `diagnostics_channel.subscribe(name, fn)` shortcut
* `tracingChannel(name)` publishes `start`, `end`, `asyncStart`, `asyncEnd` and `error` events around an operation

### Built-in channels
Node publishes channels for core modules, for example `http.client.request.start`, `http.server.request.start`, `net.client.socket`, and `undici:request:create` for fetch. Tools like OpenTelemetry, Datadog and Sentry subscribe to them.

### Related tools in the same family

|---|---|
| `AsyncLocalStorage` (`async_hooks`) | Per-request context (request id) across async calls |
| `perf_hooks` | Timing |
| `process.report`, `--heapsnapshot-signal` | Diagnostic reports and heap dumps |
| `v8.getHeapStatistics()` | Memory numbers |
| `inspector` | Programmatic debugger/profiler |

### Should you use it?
As an app developer you will mostly use it indirectly through APM tools. Library authors use it to expose events cleanly.

topics.title: Callbacks and the Error-First Pattern
topics.summary: The original async style in Node: pass a function that receives (err, result), and avoid callback hell.
topics.description:
Early Node did all asynchronous work with **callbacks**: a function you pass in that Node calls later when the operation finishes.

### The error-first convention
Node callbacks always take the error as the **first** argument and the result second:

`fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => { if (err) return handle(err); use(data); })`

If `err` is `null` or `undefined` the operation succeeded. Always check it first and `return` so you do not continue.

### Rules of good callback APIs
1. The callback is called **once**
2. The callback is called **either always sync or always async** (never mixed; "releasing Zalgo")
3. Errors are never thrown, they are passed to the callback

### Callback hell
Dependent steps nest deeper and deeper: read a file, parse it, query a database, write a result. The code drifts to the right, error handling is repeated at each level and it is easy to forget a `return`.

### Escape routes
* Name your functions and keep them flat
* Wrap callbacks with `util.promisify` and use `async/await`

### Where you still see them

topics.title: Promises in Node
topics.summary: Promises represent a future value, can be chained and combined with Promise.all, allSettled, race and any.
topics.description:
A **Promise** is an object for a value that will exist later. It has three states: *pending*, *fulfilled* (with a value) or *rejected* (with an error). Once settled it never changes.

### Using promises
`fetchUser(1).then(user => user.name).catch(err => ...).finally(() => ...)`. Each `.then` returns a **new** promise, so you can chain. Returning a value passes it on; returning a promise waits for it; throwing becomes a rejection.

### Creating promises
`new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })` wraps callback APIs. Call `resolve` or `reject` exactly once. Most of the time you can use `util.promisify` or the built-in promise APIs instead of writing this by hand.

### Combinators
| Function | Result |
|---|---|
| `Promise.all([...])` | All values; rejects at the first failure |
| `Promise.allSettled([...])` | Waits for all; gives `{status, value/reason}` for each |
| `Promise.race([...])` | First to settle (value or error) |
| `Promise.any([...])` | First to **fulfil**; rejects only if all fail |
| `Promise.withResolvers()` | `{ promise, resolve, reject }` handy for events |

### Parallel vs sequential
Starting promises first and awaiting later runs them in parallel: `await Promise.all([a(), b()])`. Awaiting one after another runs them in sequence and takes the sum of both durations.

### Unhandled rejections
A rejected promise with no handler triggers `unhandledRejection`. Since Node 15 this **crashes the process** by default.

### Microtasks
`.then` callbacks run as microtasks, after the current synchronous code and before timers.

topics.summary: Write asynchronous code that reads like synchronous code, and control parallelism, retries and timeouts.
topics.description:
`async` functions always return a promise. Inside them, `await` pauses **that function** (not the whole program) until the promise settles. The event loop keeps serving other work in the meantime.

### Error handling
Use `try/catch/finally` around awaits. A rejected promise throws at the `await` line.

### Sequential vs parallel
Slow: `const a = await getA(); const b = await getB();` (sum of times).
Fast: `const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]);` (the longer of the two).

### await in loops
`for (const id of ids) await load(id)` is **sequential**. `forEach(async ...)` does not wait at all. For parallel use `Promise.all(ids.map(load))`. For huge lists limit concurrency (batches, `p-limit`, or a small queue) so you do not open thousands of connections at once.

### Top-level await
Available in ES modules, so scripts can `await` directly without wrapping in `main()`.

### Common patterns
* **Timeout**: `Promise.race([work(), rejectAfter(ms)])`, better with `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`
* **Retry with backoff**: loop with `await sleep(2 ** attempt * 100)`
* **Async iteration**: `for await (const chunk of stream)`
* **Fire and forget**: call without await but always attach `.catch(log)`

### Return await
Inside `try/catch` use `return await fn()`; without `await` a rejection escapes your catch.

topics.title: The Event Loop in Depth
topics.summary: The six libuv phases (timers, pending, idle/prepare, poll, check, close) and how Node decides what to run next.
topics.description:
The **event loop** is what lets one thread handle thousands of concurrent tasks. After your main script finishes, Node enters the loop and keeps cycling through **phases**. Each phase has a queue of callbacks.

### The phases in order
1. **timers**: runs expired `setTimeout` / `setInterval` callbacks
2. **pending callbacks**: some deferred system callbacks (e.g. certain TCP errors)
3. **idle, prepare**: internal use
4. **poll**: retrieves new I/O events and runs their callbacks (file reads, sockets, HTTP). If nothing is queued it may **wait here** for I/O (but not past the next timer, and not if `setImmediate` callbacks are waiting)
5. **check**: runs `setImmediate` callbacks
6. **close callbacks**: e.g. `socket.on('close')`

Between **every callback** (since Node 11), Node drains the `process.nextTick` queue and then the promise microtask queue.

### Who does the real work?
* Network I/O uses the OS (epoll, kqueue, IOCP): no extra threads
* File system, DNS lookup, crypto, zlib use the **libuv thread pool** (4 threads by default, `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` up to 1024)
* Results are delivered back to the loop as callbacks

### The loop ends when nothing is left
No pending timers, handles, requests or servers: the process exits. An open server or `setInterval` keeps it alive.

### Blocking the loop
Any long synchronous work in a callback delays **everything**: timers fire late, requests stall. Typical culprits: large `JSON.parse`, regex catastrophes, sync fs/crypto, big loops.

### Quick intuition
timers → poll (I/O) → check (setImmediate) → close, repeated forever, with microtasks drained after each callback.

topics.title: nextTick vs Microtasks vs setImmediate
topics.summary: The precise execution order of synchronous code, nextTick, promises, timers and setImmediate.
topics.description:
Several APIs let you "run this soon". Their order is a classic interview topic.

### The priority order
1. **Synchronous code** of the current script
2. **`process.nextTick` queue**
3. **Promise microtasks** (`.then`, `await` continuations, `queueMicrotask`)
4. **Macrotasks** in event loop phases: timers, I/O callbacks, `setImmediate`

After each macrotask callback, Node drains nextTick first and then the microtask queue, and repeats until both are empty.

### Details
* `nextTick` is Node-specific and runs before promise callbacks (in CommonJS). In an **ES module** the top-level code itself runs as a microtask, so promise callbacks queued there run **before** nextTick callbacks. Inside later callbacks (timers, I/O) the CommonJS order applies.
* `setTimeout(fn, 0)` vs `setImmediate(fn)` in the main module is **not deterministic** (depends on process speed). Inside an I/O callback `setImmediate` always wins.
* `setImmediate` runs in the check phase after poll; `setTimeout` runs in the timers phase.

### Starvation
A recursive `process.nextTick` (or endless microtasks) never lets the loop move to I/O or timers, freezing the program. `setImmediate` recursion is safe because the loop runs between calls.

### Use cases
* `nextTick`: emit an event after the constructor returns, so listeners can attach
* `setImmediate`: yield to I/O in a long computation, split work into chunks
* `queueMicrotask`: schedule small follow-up work

### await and ordering
`await x` continues in a microtask, so code after `await` runs before any timer.

topics.title: Streams: Readable, Writable, Transform
topics.summary: Process data in chunks instead of loading it all: the four stream types, modes and async iteration.
topics.description:
A **stream** processes data piece by piece, so you can handle files larger than memory and start sending output before all input has arrived. Streams are everywhere in Node: `fs`, `http` requests/responses, `net` sockets, `zlib`, `process.stdin/stdout`.

### Four kinds
| Type | Direction | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Readable** | source | `fs.createReadStream`, `http.IncomingMessage`, `process.stdin` |
| **Writable** | destination | `fs.createWriteStream`, `http.ServerResponse`, `process.stdout` |
| **Duplex** | both, independent | TCP socket |
| **Transform** | Duplex that modifies data | `zlib.createGzip()`, crypto ciphers |

### Reading from a Readable
* Async iterator (best): `for await (const chunk of readable) { ... }`
* Events: `'data'`, `'end'`, `'error'`, `'close'`
* `readable.pipe(writable)` (older) or `pipeline()` (preferred)

### Writing
`writable.write(chunk)` returns a boolean. `writable.end()` finishes the stream and fires `'finish'`.

### Chunk types
Chunks are `Buffer` (or strings with an encoding). With `objectMode: true` chunks can be any JS value, handy for parsing pipelines.

### Create your own
`new Transform({ transform(chunk, enc, cb) { cb(null, chunk.toString().toUpperCase()); } })` or with an async generator: `Readable.from(asyncGenerator())`.

### Web Streams
Node also implements the browser `ReadableStream` API (used by `fetch` bodies). Convert with `Readable.fromWeb` and `Readable.toWeb`.

### Why it matters
Copying a 4 GB file with `readFile` needs 4 GB of RAM. A stream needs roughly 64 KB at a time.

topics.title: Backpressure and pipeline
topics.summary: How streams slow a fast producer for a slow consumer, and why pipeline beats pipe for error handling.
topics.description:
If a source produces data faster than the destination can consume it (a fast disk and a slow network client), the extra data piles up in memory. **Backpressure** is the mechanism that tells the producer to pause.

### How it works
Every stream has an internal buffer limited by `highWaterMark` (16 KB default, 64 KB for fs streams, 16 objects in objectMode).
* `writable.write(chunk)` returns **`false`** when the buffer is full
* Stop writing and wait for the `'drain'` event
* `readable.pause()` and `resume()` control the flow on the reading side

Hand-written version:
`if (!res.write(chunk)) { readable.pause(); res.once('drain', () => readable.resume()); }`

### pipe handles it, but...
`readable.pipe(writable)` applies backpressure automatically but has weak error handling: if one stream errors, the others are **not destroyed** and file descriptors leak.

### Use pipeline
`stream.pipeline(a, b, c, cb)` or the promise version `await pipeline(a, b, c)` from `node:stream/promises`:
* Connects the streams with backpressure
* On any error, **destroys all** streams and reports the error once
* Resolves when the last stream finishes
* Accepts async generator functions in the middle as transforms

### Async generators as transforms
`await pipeline(source, async function* (chunks) { for await (const c of chunks) yield c.toString().toUpperCase(); }, destination)`

### Compose and finished
`stream.compose()` joins streams into a single duplex. `stream.finished()` (or `finished` promise) waits for a stream to end or fail.

### Diagnosing memory growth
If memory grows steadily while piping, someone is writing without respecting `drain` (for example a loop calling `write` hundreds of thousands of times).

topics.title: AbortController and Cancellation
topics.summary: Cancel fetch, timers, streams, child processes and your own async work with AbortSignal, including timeouts.
topics.description:
**`AbortController`** is the standard way to cancel asynchronous operations. The same API exists in browsers.

### Parts
* `const ac = new AbortController()`
* `ac.signal` is an `AbortSignal` you pass to cancellable APIs
* `ac.abort(reason?)` triggers cancellation; the signal's `aborted` becomes `true` and an `abort` event fires

### Who accepts a signal?
`fetch`, `fs.readFile` / `fs.watch` / `writeFile`, `timers/promises`, `child_process`, `events.once`, `stream.pipeline`, `http.request`, `readline`, `net`, `dns/promises`, and many libraries (axios, undici, database drivers).

### Handy helpers
* `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` aborts automatically after a delay (rejects with `TimeoutError`)
* `AbortSignal.any([s1, s2])` aborts when any signal aborts (user cancel **or** timeout)
* `signal.throwIfAborted()` checks inside your own loops

### Cancelled operations reject
They reject with an `AbortError` (`err.name === 'AbortError'`). Treat that as expected, not as a failure to log loudly.

### Make your own functions cancellable
Accept `{ signal }` as an option, check `signal.aborted` between steps, listen with `signal.addEventListener('abort', cleanup, { once: true })` and pass the signal on to the APIs you call.

### Use cases in servers
Cancel database queries and upstream requests when the client disconnects; enforce per-request timeouts; stop watchers and background loops during shutdown.

topics.title: Error Handling in Async Code
topics.summary: Handle rejections, uncaught exceptions and operational errors correctly so one bug does not silently corrupt your server.
topics.description:
### Two kinds of errors
* **Operational errors**: expected runtime problems (network down, file missing, invalid input, DB timeout). Handle and respond.
* **Programmer errors**: bugs (`undefined is not a function`). Fix the code; the safest reaction is to log and restart.

### Rules for promises and async/await
1. Every promise chain ends with `.catch()` or sits inside `try/catch` with `await`.
2. Return or await promises; a "floating" promise's error becomes an `unhandledRejection`.
3. Throw `Error` objects (they have stack traces), never strings. Use `new Error('msg', { cause: err })` to keep the original error.
4. In a `Promise.all` all other promises keep running even though the first rejection settles the result.

### Global safety nets (last resort)
`process.on('unhandledRejection', ...)` and `process.on('uncaughtException', ...)`. After an uncaught exception the process state is unknown. **Log and exit**, and let a process manager (PM2, Docker, Kubernetes) restart it. Do not keep running.

### Callbacks and event emitters
Errors in callbacks are passed as the first argument. Emitters need an `'error'` listener. `try/catch` around them does nothing.

### Custom error classes
Create `class AppError extends Error { constructor(msg, status) { super(msg); this.status = status; } }` so you can map errors to HTTP status codes in a central handler.

### Express
Express 5 forwards rejected promises from async handlers to the error middleware automatically. In Express 4 you must wrap handlers or call `next(err)`.

### Never swallow errors
An empty `catch {}` hides bugs. Log at least and decide: retry, return a friendly error or rethrow.

interview.a: Log the error, close resources if possible and exit with a non-zero code. Rely on a supervisor (PM2, systemd, Docker, Kubernetes) to restart; continuing can leave the app in a corrupt state.

topics.title: Not Blocking the Event Loop
topics.summary: Recognise CPU-heavy synchronous code that freezes your server and break it up, offload it or stream it.
topics.description:
One slow synchronous task freezes **every connected client**, because there is only one JavaScript thread. A healthy Node service keeps each callback short (a few milliseconds).

### Typical blockers
* Sync APIs in handlers: `readFileSync`, `execSync`, `pbkdf2Sync`, `zlib.gzipSync`
* Big loops, sorting millions of items, heavy recursion
* `JSON.parse` / `JSON.stringify` on very large payloads
* **ReDoS**: a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking on user input
* Large `Buffer` and string operations, `replace` on huge text

### Symptoms
High latency for all routes, health checks timing out, timers firing late, CPU at 100% on one core. Measure with `monitorEventLoopDelay` or `clinic doctor`.

### Strategies
| Strategy | How |
|---|---|
| Partition | Process in chunks and yield with `await setImmediate()` between chunks |
| Offload | `worker_threads` pool (piscina), or another service |
| Stream | Parse big payloads incrementally (stream-json, ndjson) |
| Use async APIs | `fs.promises`, `crypto.pbkdf2` (thread pool) |
| Limit input | Max body size, safe regexes (`safe-regex`, RE2) |
| Queue | Move heavy jobs to a background worker (BullMQ) |

### Fairness trick
`import { setImmediate as yieldLoop } from 'node:timers/promises'` then `await yieldLoop()` every N iterations lets pending I/O run.

### Rule of thumb
If a task takes more than about 50 ms of pure CPU, do not run it directly on the request path.
